clinicalPearls: An abnormal congenital communication between the trachea and oesophagus, most often occurring together with oesophageal atresia; the commonest anatomical type is proximal oesophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.
Typical newborn features include excessive drooling and frothy secretions, choking, coughing, and cyanosis with feeds, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube into the stomach.

A characteristic radiographic clue is a feeding tube coiling in the upper oesophageal pouch; gas in the stomach and bowel indicates a distal fistula, while a gasless abdomen suggests atresia without a distal fistula.
Aspiration of saliva and, via the fistula, gastric contents into the airway causes respiratory compromise and pneumonitis.
An isolated H-type fistula without atresia may present later with recurrent coughing during feeds, cyanotic spells, and recurrent respiratory infections.
Initial management protects the airway and lungs: keep the infant nil by mouth, apply continuous suction to the upper pouch, and position to reduce aspiration and reflux through the fistula.
It is frequently part of the VACTERL association, so evaluation for vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies is important.
Definitive treatment is surgical division of the fistula and repair of the oesophageal atresia, timed according to the infant's stability and anatomy.
Long-term issues can include anastomotic stricture, gastro-oesophageal reflux, tracheomalacia, and dysphagia requiring ongoing follow-up.
reference.pathophysiology: Abnormal separation of the primitive foregut into trachea and oesophagus during embryogenesis leaves an abnormal connection between the two and, commonly, a discontinuous oesophagus (atresia). In the common configuration, the upper oesophagus ends in a blind pouch while the lower oesophagus connects to the trachea. Swallowed secretions collect in and overflow from the upper pouch into the airway, and the distal fistula allows gastric contents to reflux into the trachea and air to distend the stomach. These mechanisms produce aspiration, chemical pneumonitis, and, with a large distal fistula, gaseous abdominal distension that further impairs ventilation.
additionalInvestigations: Attempted passage of a nasogastric tube with radiograph showing tube coiling in the upper pouch
Chest and abdominal radiograph to assess the pouch and bowel gas pattern
Echocardiography to identify cardiac anomalies and aortic arch side before surgery
Renal ultrasound and spinal and limb assessment for VACTERL anomalies
Bronchoscopy or contrast study to define an H-type fistula when suspected
redFlags: Choking, cyanosis, and respiratory distress with attempted feeding
Aspiration pneumonitis from overflow of secretions or reflux through the fistula
Progressive gastric and bowel distension impairing ventilation via a large distal fistula
Recurrent respiratory infections and cyanotic spells suggesting a missed H-type fistula
Associated critical cardiac or other major anomalies within the VACTERL spectrum
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and surgical repair the outlook is generally favourable, and prognosis is influenced strongly by prematurity, birth weight, and associated anomalies, particularly cardiac lesions. Many children require management of later complications such as strictures, reflux, and tracheomalacia but achieve good long-term function.
pitfalls: Feeding a newborn with excessive drooling before excluding oesophageal atresia, precipitating aspiration
Missing a delayed-presenting H-type fistula in a child with recurrent feeding-related respiratory symptoms
Failing to search for associated VACTERL anomalies, especially cardiac lesions, before surgery
Overlooking that a gasless abdomen indicates atresia without a distal fistula
Underestimating long-term reflux, stricture, and tracheomalacia complications requiring follow-up
